reference.source: ATLS / Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine (critical care)
clinicalPearls: Recognise failure clinically before blood gases confirm it: rising respiratory rate, accessory muscle use, altered consciousness, and inability to speak in full sentences are early warnings
Type 1 (hypoxaemic) failure reflects a problem with oxygenation, whereas type 2 (hypercapnic) failure reflects inadequate ventilation and carbon dioxide clearance
Secure the airway and support oxygenation and ventilation as the first priority, in parallel with seeking the cause
A falling respiratory rate or conscious level in a tiring patient can herald impending arrest rather than improvement
Non-invasive ventilation can be effective in selected causes, but a deteriorating or obtunded patient needs intubation without delay
Titrate oxygen to a target saturation, being mindful of the risk of worsening hypercapnia in chronic carbon dioxide retainers
Arterial blood gases distinguish the type of failure and reveal the acid-base disturbance guiding urgency
Treat the reversible precipitant (e.g. bronchospasm, pulmonary oedema, pneumothorax) alongside respiratory support
reference.pathophysiology: Respiratory failure occurs when gas exchange fails to maintain adequate oxygenation or carbon dioxide elimination. Hypoxaemic (type 1) failure arises mainly from ventilation-perfusion mismatch and shunt, as in pneumonia, pulmonary oedema, and acute respiratory distress syndrome, where alveoli are filled or collapsed. Hypercapnic (type 2) failure results from reduced alveolar ventilation due to depressed respiratory drive, neuromuscular weakness, increased airway resistance, or chest wall problems, so carbon dioxide accumulates. Both cause tissue hypoxia; hypercapnia additionally produces respiratory acidosis. Fatigue of the respiratory muscles can convert a compensated state into rapid decompensation and arrest.
additionalDifferentials: Acute exacerbation of asthma or COPD
Neuromuscular weakness or central respiratory depression
additionalInvestigations: Arterial blood gas to classify the type of failure and assess acid-base status
Chest radiograph to identify consolidation, oedema, effusion, or pneumothorax
Continuous pulse oximetry and capnography where available
Bedside lung and cardiac ultrasound to differentiate causes
CT pulmonary angiography if embolism is suspected
redFlags: Exhaustion with a falling respiratory rate or rising carbon dioxide indicating impending respiratory arrest
Deteriorating conscious level or inability to protect the airway
Refractory hypoxaemia despite maximal oxygen therapy
Silent chest or minimal air entry in severe bronchospasm
Haemodynamic instability accompanying the respiratory compromise
reference.prognosis: Prognosis depends on the underlying cause and reversibility. Prompt recognition and support of oxygenation and ventilation with treatment of the precipitant allow recovery in many cases, whereas established acute respiratory distress syndrome and multi-organ involvement carry substantial mortality.
pitfalls: Mistaking a tiring patient's slowing respiratory rate for clinical improvement
Uncontrolled high-flow oxygen worsening hypercapnia in chronic retainers
Persisting with non-invasive ventilation in a patient who needs intubation
Treating the numbers on the blood gas without addressing the underlying cause
Underestimating fatigue and delaying escalation of respiratory support
management: Secure the airway and support oxygenation and ventilation as the immediate priority
Controlled oxygen therapy titrated to a target saturation, cautiously in chronic carbon dioxide retainers
Non-invasive ventilation for selected causes such as hypercapnic COPD exacerbation or cardiogenic pulmonary oedema
Invasive mechanical ventilation for the obtunded or deteriorating patient without delay
Identify and treat the underlying precipitant, for example antibiotics for pneumonia, diuretics for pulmonary oedema, and bronchodilators for airflow obstruction
Monitor with arterial blood gases, continuous pulse oximetry, and capnography
Escalate to intensive care for organ support and refractory hypoxaemia
